evidence.role: Dependency retrieval is grounded in the verified Lesson 1 handoff; P2 leaves establish why complete unit-bearing estimates matter

hints: Recall what the number in a measurement record tells you.
Then name the part written beside the number that gives its measurement scale.

walkthrough.text: Recall the structure established in Lesson 1 for every physical quantity.
The number is the numerical magnitude and states how much.
The unit states the measurement scale, so the two parts are numerical magnitude and unit.

ai_rubric.observable: States numerical magnitude or numerical value
States unit

evidence.role: Mapped P2 mass-estimation demand informs scale selection; the school-bag context, values and options are original

hints: Compare the bag with familiar objects whose masses are around one kilogram.
Reject any option that one student could not realistically carry or that is lighter than the bag's contents.

walkthrough.text: A loaded school bag contains several substantial objects, so a few thousandths of a kilogram is far too small.
A mass of 500 kg is far too large for one student to lift.
A loaded bag commonly has a mass of several kilograms, so 5 kg has the believable scale and C is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects 5 kg as a reasonable mass estimate for a loaded school bag

evidence.role: P2 evidence grounds the requirement to choose a defensible physical scale; the time context is original

hints: A blink is visible but lasts much less than one full second.
Choose the option that is a fraction of a second rather than many seconds or an almost instantaneous interval.

walkthrough.text: One blink is a quick closing and opening movement, so it should take less than one second.
Values of 20 s and 2000 s are far too long, while 0.002 s is too short for the full visible movement.
A few tenths of a second is believable, so 0.2 s and option B are correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects 0.2 s as a reasonable time estimate for one blink

evidence.role: Mapped P2 evidence directly grounds hand-sized-object volume estimation; object, benchmark, values and wording are original

hints: First estimate the volume of the 5 cm cube by multiplying its three side lengths.
Choose an apple volume on the same scale as that cube, with a modest allowance for the apple's size and shape.

walkthrough.text: The benchmark cube has volume 5 cm x 5 cm x 5 cm = 125 cm³.
A large apple should have a volume near this benchmark, not one hundredth or one hundred times its value.
The nearby option 150 cm³ is reasonable, so C is correct.

ai_rubric.observable: Selects 150 cm³ as a reasonable volume estimate for a large apple

evidence.role: The direct P2 estimation leaves establish acceptance of a physically justified range; the door and benchmark reasoning are original

hints: Choose a familiar object or person whose height you know roughly.
Decide whether a classroom door is shorter than, similar to or taller than that benchmark before stating a value in metres.

walkthrough.text: A student height is a relevant benchmark because it is measured in the same direction and is familiar.
A classroom door must be a little taller than most students so that they can walk through it comfortably.
This comparison supports a door-height estimate near 2 m. Values from 1.8 m to 2.5 m are defensible when the comparison is sensible.
Attach m to the numerical magnitude because the prompt requests a height in metres.

ai_rubric.observable: Names a physically relevant height or length benchmark
Compares the classroom door sensibly with the chosen benchmark
States a justified door-height estimate from 1.8 m to 2.5 m
Includes m as the unit of the estimated height

evidence.role: Mass-estimation demand is evidence-grounded; the grouped-book calculation, data and figure brief are original

hints: Use the estimated mass for one book once for each of the 12 identical books.
After calculating, ask whether one person could lift a bundle on that scale and remember that the starting single-book value was approximate.

walkthrough.text: The books are identical, so scale the single-book estimate by the number of books.
Estimated bundle mass = 12 x 0.25 kg = 3.0 kg.
Because 0.25 kg was only an estimate, the bundle result should be reported honestly as about 3 kg rather than as an exact measurement.
A bundle of 12 books should feel much heavier than one book but remain liftable by one person. A mass of a few kilograms fits that physical comparison.
Arithmetic check: four books would be about 1 kg, so three groups of four books would be about 3 kg.

ai_rubric.observable: Multiplies the estimated single-book mass by 12
Obtains and reports the bundle mass as about 3 kg
Explains that the result remains approximate because 0.25 kg is an estimated benchmark
Gives a relevant physical comparison for a bundle of 12 books
Uses the physical comparison to support a mass on the scale of a few kilograms

evidence.role: The mapped P2 leaf grounds volume estimation in cm³; the box geometry, dimensions, dependency demand and figure brief are original

hints: Multiply the three perpendicular approximate dimensions and keep their shared centimetre scale attached to the volume.
For the check, calculate the volume of one 10 cm cube and compare the box volume with that cube-volume.

walkthrough.text: Use the three approximate dimensions: estimated volume = 40 cm x 30 cm x 25 cm.
Multiplication gives 40 x 30 x 25 = 30 000, so the estimated volume is 30 000 cm³.
The numerical magnitude is 30 000 and the unit is cm³. The bare number would omit the measurement unit and would not completely report the physical quantity.
A 10 cm cube has volume 10 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm = 1000 cm³.

Compare volumes directly: 30 000 cm³ / 1000 cm³ = 30, so the box volume is equivalent to 30 of the 10 cm cube-volumes. This is a volume ratio, not a claim that 30 rigid cubes pack exactly inside the box.
The check gives 30 x 1000 cm³ = 30 000 cm³, confirming the scale of the estimate.

ai_rubric.observable: Multiplies the three approximate dimensions 40 cm, 30 cm and 25 cm
Obtains the estimated box volume as 30 000 cm³
Identifies 30 000 as the numerical magnitude and cm³ as the unit
Explains that the bare number is incomplete because it does not state the measurement unit
Uses a 10 cm cube as 1000 cm³ and shows that the box volume is equivalent to 30 such cube-volumes
Shows that the cube check gives the same scale of 30 000 cm³

audit.originality: All learner contexts, wording, values and planned diagrams are original. No official wording, numbers or visual layouts were reproduced.
audit.scope: Reasonable estimation of physical quantities using familiar benchmarks, scale bracketing, appropriate units and plausibility checks.
audit.evidence: All three mapped P2 leaves, their complete source questions and official marking demands were reviewed. P1 evidence is deferred and was not inferred.
